description: Let’s do something different, like we used to imagine when we were kids.
summary: SitaRam is a web app that helps astronauts assess their own health on long missions. It addresses the challenge by letting astronauts gather their own health indicators, understand what they mean, and get guidance on what to do.Astronauts track heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, blood pressure, blood sugar, sleep, exercise, and radiation, plus mood, stress, and fatigue through a daily check-in. Readings are color-coded and compared with each astronaut's own usual level, giving early warnings. A clickable body map breaks the body into parts and components, explains how spaceflight affects each one, and offers a quick symptom check with guidance. SitaRam reminds astronauts when measurements are due, gives tips for a station, spacecraft, rover, or Moon/Mars base, turns a prescription into a medicine schedule, and raises an emergency alert to the crew and ground if the astronaut does not respond. It is organised around NASA's five hazards of spaceflight. It matters because, far from Earth, astronauts must spot problems early and act on their own.
details:
SitaRam is a single-page web prototype. Intended impact: to help astronauts catch problems early and act on their own when Earth is too far for quick help, and to make health assessment simple enough for non-experts."

"Factors considered: astronauts are not medical experts, so every reading comes with plain explanations and color coding. Distance from Earth means the app cannot wait for ground, so it works on its own. Mental health matters as much as physical health, so there is a daily mood, stress, and fatigue check-in. Safety: the app states it is guidance only and tells astronauts when to contact the flight surgeon.An astronaut sees live, color-coded readings with trend lines. Each reading is compared with their own recent level, so a drift is flagged even when the value is still in the normal range. Readings can be simulated, typed in, or loaded from a CSV file. A clickable body map lists the components of each part (for example hands: skin, muscles, bones, nerves), explains the space effects, and runs a quick symptom check with mild, moderate, or urgent guidance. A "Contact flight surgeon" flow prepares a case summary and turns the doctor's advice into a care plan. Prescription photos are read with open-source text recognition and turned into a schedule. If an astronaut is unresponsive after an urgent alert, the app alerts the crew and drafts a message to ground. A section on NASA's five hazards links each hazard to the readings affected.

Benefits and impact: astronauts can act early without waiting for Earth, which matters most on long missions with communication delays.

Tools: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages, with Tesseract.js for text recognition.

Limits (honest): this is a prototype. Data is simulated, alert limits are illustrative, and it is not a medical device. The crew and ground alerts are simulated. Real sensors, official medical limits, and offline operation are next steps.

Creativity: a body map that drills down into each body part, plus the personal-baseline early warnings.

AI use: code, descriptive text, and sample data were generated with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic).
